claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential trained on strategically selected ab initio free-energy calculations can accurately reproduce solid and liquid free energies at high temperatures.
The training data can incorporate anharmonic and electron–vibration effects.
The proposed MLIP can reproduce derived properties such as melting temperature.
The proposed MLIP workflow will substantially reduce computational cost relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
Elemental and binary systems with reliable ab initio molar-volume, elastic-constant, and vibrational-spectrum data provide the proposed initial test domain.
The MLIP training set will cover configurations from both solid and liquid phases.
Perturbative corrections will be added to represent electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic vibrational entropy.
Combining the MLIP with nested sampling or Monte Carlo methods will permit evaluation of phase free energies.
The proposed tests span temperatures below, at, and above melting for elemental and binary systems.
The MLIP will mediate between ab initio electronic-structure outputs and bulk thermodynamic properties by reproducing the potential-energy surface.
The reproduced potential-energy surface will include local relaxations and anharmonic effects.
Training on diverse free-energy configurations, vibrational modes, and electron–vibration corrections will enable the model to represent the free-energy landscapes of both solid and liquid phases.
Representing both phase free-energy landscapes with the MLIP will reduce the need for time-consuming ab initio molecular dynamics while retaining high thermodynamic fidelity.
The MLIP workflow is expected to produce free energies and melting parameters within a few percent of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The MLIP workflow is expected to be 10–100 times faster than traditional ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD provide high fidelity but are computationally expensive for the targeted calculations.
Extension from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent alloys with up to five components may face additional challenges from configurational disorder and local relaxation.
The MLIP's ability to capture subtle electron–vibration coupling and anharmonicity over a broad temperature range is not established, especially for multicomponent systems.
